title: Residents vote on the upgrading budget
issue: Has letting residents vote on the budget led to better decisions for the estate?
background:
A town council set aside $500,000 of its yearly improvement budget for residents to decide. Residents proposed projects. Every household could then vote, online or at a booth beside the market, over two weeks in March.

The three projects with the most votes were built: a covered walkway, a fitness corner and a new playground. About one in seven households voted. The council is now deciding whether to hold the vote again next year with a bigger sum.

Study the sources to find out whether letting residents vote has led to better decisions for the estate.

sources.provenance: A poster by the town council, put up at lift lobbies before the vote.
sources.text:
Your estate. Your say.
This year YOU decide how $500,000 is spent.
Propose a project. Vote for three. Every household has one vote.
The projects with the most votes will be built. It is that simple.
Voting is open 1–14 March, online or at the booth beside the market.

sources.provenance: A resident who proposed the covered walkway, speaking at a residents' meeting after the results were announced.
sources.text: For six years we asked for a covered walkway from Block 214 to the bus stop. Nothing happened. This time we knocked on doors, got our neighbours to vote, and it came first. For once the people who use the path decided, not an office that has never walked it in the rain.

sources.provenance: A letter from an elderly resident to the town council, a month after the vote.
sources.text: I am 78 and I do not use a smartphone. I learnt about the vote only when I saw workmen at the playground. The booth was at the market for two weeks, but nobody told us at Block 230. The blocks with young families and big chat groups got what they wanted. Our broken ramp, which wheelchair users need every day, got 41 votes and nothing.

sources.provenance: From the town council's yearly report to residents, published three months after the vote.
sources.text: The budget vote was a great success. 2,140 households took part, far more than attend our meetings in a whole year. All three winning projects were completed on time and within budget. Residents have told us they feel heard. We plan to double the sum next year.

sources.provenance: From a study by university researchers, who surveyed 600 households in the estate after the vote.
sources.text: One in seven households voted. Among households with children, one in four voted; among residents aged 70 and above, one in twenty. The three winning projects were all within 300 metres of the blocks that voted most. Yet 68% of those surveyed, including many who did not vote, said the vote was a fairer way to decide than before. Most asked for paper voting forms next time.

sources.provenance: An engineer who works for the town council, interviewed for a community newsletter.
sources.text: The walkway and the fitness corner are well used. But the vote cannot see everything. The ramp at Block 230 and the old water pipes under Block 208 are urgent, and they will never win a popularity contest. If all the budget went to a vote, the things nobody notices until they fail would be left out. A vote is good for choosing between nice things, not for deciding what is necessary.

questions.question: Study Source A. What is the message of this poster? Explain your answer.

seeded.text: Source A tells me that residents can vote from 1 to 14 March, online or at the booth beside the market, and that every household has one vote.
The message is that residents now have real power over how the money for the estate is spent.

The message is that residents now have real power over how the money for the estate is spent. The poster says 'This year YOU decide how $500,000 is spent' and promises 'The projects with the most votes will be built'. The capital letters and the firm promise show that the choice belongs to the residents and not to the council. It is speaking to every household in the estate. It wants them to believe that their vote counts, so that they take part.
